sections.title: A train crosses the mountains
sections.intro_md:
On **6 June 2025** a blue and white Vande Bharat train left Katra, at the foot of the Trikuta hills, and ran north through the Pir Panjal range to **Srinagar**. For the first time, the Kashmir Valley was joined to the rest of India's rail network.

The line had taken decades. The Udhampur to Baramulla stretch alone runs about **272 km**, much of it inside the mountain: the Railways ministry counts 36 tunnels totalling about 119 km and more than 900 bridges. The tallest of them crosses the **Chenab** gorge in Reasi district, its deck higher above the river than the top of the Eiffel Tower.

Until then, the Valley's lifeline was a single highway over the Banihal pass, closed for days at a time by snow and landslides. Apples rotted in stuck trucks; families planned weddings around the weather.

That is Jammu and Kashmir in one image: a beautiful, cut-off place that the rest of the country has always found hard to reach, and harder to understand.

spotlights.name: Chenab Rail Bridge
spotlights.when: Completed August 2022, opened to trains 6 June 2025
spotlights.spot_it: A single huge steel arch springing from both sides of a deep green gorge, the rail deck running flat across its crown.
spotlights.story_md: The deck stands **359 m** above the Chenab riverbed, about 35 m higher than the top of the Eiffel Tower, which makes it the highest railway bridge in the world. The main arch spans **467 m** and the whole bridge runs 1,315 m. Engineers designed it for winds of 266 km/h, earthquakes up to magnitude 8, temperatures of minus 20 °C, and a blast of about 40 tonnes of TNT, with help from the DRDO. Work stopped in 2008 over safety worries and restarted in 2010; the two half arches, cantilevered out from each bank with cables, finally met in April 2021. About 28,660 tonnes of steel went in. A few kilometres away, the **Anji Khad** bridge, India's first cable-stayed railway bridge, carries the same line 186 m over another gorge.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the engineering that finally put the Kashmir Valley on India's rail map.
spotlights.memory_hook: Higher than the Eiffel Tower, built to survive a bomb.

sections.title: Two capitals, one valley, and a lot of mountains
sections.intro_md:
**Jammu and Kashmir** became a **union territory** on **31 October 2019**, when Parliament split the old state in two and made Ladakh a separate territory. It has an elected assembly of 90 seats, a chief minister (**Omar Abdullah**, since 16 October 2024) and a Lieutenant Governor appointed by Delhi (**Manoj Sinha**), who controls police and public order.

The territory has **20 districts** in two divisions of 10 each. **Kashmir** is a flat-floored valley about 135 km long, ringed by the Himalaya and the Pir Panjal, Muslim-majority and Kashmiri-speaking. **Jammu** is the hill country and plain to the south, sloping down to Punjab, with a Hindu majority, Dogri speech and a Dogra royal past. Between and around them live Gujjar and Bakarwal herders and Pahari-speaking hill people.

The 2011 census counted **12.27 million** people: about 68% Muslim, 28% Hindu and 2% Sikh. India's official map counts land that Pakistan administers, so official area figures run far above what Delhi actually governs. The numbers below are the ones that matter.

spotlights.name: Srinagar
spotlights.when: Founded, by tradition, under the Mauryas; capital since the 7th century
spotlights.spot_it: Old wooden and brick houses with pitched tin roofs lining the Jhelum, crossed by numbered bridges called kadals.
spotlights.story_md: The summer capital sits on both banks of the **Jhelum**, crossed in the old city by a chain of bridges called **kadals**: Amira Kadal, Habba Kadal, Zaina Kadal and others, several named after the rulers who built them. Behind the river lie Dal Lake, the Mughal gardens and the Hari Parbat fort. With about 1.2 million people in its metro area, it is the largest city in the Himalaya. The old city's houses use a technique called **taq**, brick piers laced with timber, and **dhajji dewari**, timber frames filled with brick. Both flex in earthquakes, and engineers studied them after the 2005 quake knocked down concrete buildings nearby while many old houses stood.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the political, commercial and emotional centre of the Valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city counted in bridges: kadal, kadal, kadal.

spotlights.name: Jammu, the city of temples
spotlights.when: Bahu Fort tradition: 14th century; Dogra capital from 1820s
spotlights.spot_it: Temple spires above a busy hill town on the Tawi river, with the walls of Bahu Fort on the far bank.
spotlights.story_md: Jammu is the winter capital and the larger of the two cities by some counts. Local tradition says a king named **Jambu Lochan** saw a tiger and a goat drink from the **Tawi** side by side and founded a city where such peace was possible. The town grew into the seat of the **Dogra** rajas, who ruled all of Jammu and Kashmir from 1846 to 1947. Their **Raghunath temple** complex, begun by Gulab Singh and finished by Ranbir Singh in 1860, holds hundreds of stone lingams and gives the city its nickname. Most of the 9 to 10 million pilgrims bound for **Vaishno Devi** each year pass through.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the gateway to the whole territory and the heart of Dogra culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tiger and a goat at one river: so goes the founding story.

spotlights.name: Darbar Move, the capital that travels
spotlights.spot_it: Convoys of trucks loaded with government files crawling over the Banihal pass every spring and autumn.
spotlights.story_md: Since **1872**, when Maharaja **Ranbir Singh** began it, the whole government moved twice a year: to **Srinagar** for summer (May to October) and to **Jammu** for winter. Thousands of employees and truckloads of paper crossed the mountains each time. Critics called it a costly relic; defenders said it bound the two regions together and gave each a turn with the government at its door. The Lieutenant Governor's administration ended it on **30 June 2021**, saying e-files had made it pointless. The elected government brought it back: on **23 September 2025** the cabinet decided to restore it, and offices reopened in Jammu on **3 November 2025**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a 150-year-old ritual that says the territory has two centres, not one.
spotlights.memory_hook: The government that packs its bags twice a year.

sections.title: A lake bed between mountain walls
sections.intro_md:
The Kashmir Valley was once a lake. Kashmiri legend calls it **Satisar**, the lake of Sati, drained when the sage Kashyapa had a demon killed and a gap cut in the mountains; geologists agree on the lake, and point to the flat **karewa** terraces, old lake sediments, where saffron and almonds now grow. The **Jhelum** rises at the spring of Verinag, meanders through the Valley floor, feeds **Wular** and leaves through a gorge at Baramulla toward Pakistan.

To the south the **Pir Panjal** range, peaks above 4,500 m, walls the Valley off from Jammu. The Jammu side drops through the Shivalik hills to a hot plain at about 300 m; the **Chenab** and **Tawi** cut through it.

Winter in the Valley is cold and grey. The harshest 40 days, **Chillai Kalan**, run from 21 December to 29 January, when Dal Lake's edges can freeze. Spring brings almond blossom in March and tulips in April; autumn turns the chinar trees red.

spotlights.name: Dal Lake
spotlights.when: Mughal pleasure lake; houseboats from the late 19th century
spotlights.spot_it: Painted wooden shikaras with heart-shaped paddles gliding past moored houseboats, the Zabarwan hills behind.
spotlights.story_md: Dal is about **18 km²** of water, marsh and floating gardens on Srinagar's eastern edge, split by causeways into basins. Families grow tomatoes and lotus root (**nadru**) on **raadh**, floating mats of weed and mud that can be cut loose and towed. Before dawn a **floating vegetable market** trades from boat to boat. The lake is also in trouble: sewage, silt and weed have shrunk its open water, and governments have spent hundreds of crores on dredging and relocating lake dwellers. In the hardest winters its edges freeze solid enough to walk on.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the postcard of Kashmir and a living neighbourhood of 50,000-odd people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gardens that float and can be towed away.

spotlights.name: Wular Lake
spotlights.spot_it: A huge shallow sheet of water with reed beds and fishing boats, mountains of Bandipora behind.
spotlights.story_md: Wular is one of the **largest freshwater lakes in Asia**, its area swinging between about 30 and 260 km² with the season. It works as a sponge for the Jhelum, soaking up floods. Sultan **Zain-ul-Abidin** built an artificial island, **Zainalanka**, in its waters in the 1440s, with a palace and mosque. In the 1980s India began the **Tulbul** navigation project at its outlet; Pakistan objected under the Indus Waters Treaty and work stopped. Thousands of families harvest water chestnut (**singhara**) and fish here, and the lake supplies a large share of the Valley's fish.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Valley's flood buffer and fish basket.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lake that breathes in and out with the Jhelum.

spotlights.name: Gulmarg and its gondola
spotlights.spot_it: A broad meadow ringed by pines, deep in snow, with cable cars climbing toward the Apharwat ridge.
spotlights.story_md: Gulmarg, the meadow of flowers, sits at about **2,650 m**. The British made it a hill resort with one of the world's highest golf courses. Today skiers come for the **Gulmarg Gondola**, built by the French firm Pomagalski: its second stage, opened in 2005, climbs to about **3,980 m** on Apharwat, among the highest cable cars on Earth, and opens off-piste slopes that draw skiers from Europe and Australia. Gulmarg hosts the **Khelo India Winter Games**. In dry winters, such as 2024 when January passed almost without snow, the whole resort economy freezes instead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's best-known ski slope.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pines, powder and a cable car to 4,000 metres.

spotlights.name: Chinar tree
spotlights.when: Planted widely from the 14th to 17th centuries
spotlights.spot_it: A massive plane tree with five-lobed, hand-shaped leaves that turn flame red and gold in late October.
spotlights.story_md: The **chinar** (*Platanus orientalis*) came to Kashmir from West Asia, probably carried by Persian and Central Asian travellers; Sufi saints and Mughal emperors planted it everywhere. One at **Chattergam** in Budgam is often cited as among the oldest, said to be planted in the 14th century. Felling a chinar is illegal without permission and the trees are counted and geotagged by the government. Its dry leaves were once collected and burned into charcoal for the **kangri** fire pot. The leaf is the symbol of the Army's Srinagar corps, Chinar Corps.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the tree Kashmiris consider their own, though it came from Persia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Red hands waving goodbye to autumn.

spotlights.name: Hangul, the Kashmir stag
spotlights.spot_it: A red deer with a big branching rack, usually 11 to 16 points, its bugle echoing across autumn slopes.
spotlights.story_md: The hangul is Central Asia's red deer at its southern limit and the territory's state animal. A century ago there may have been **3,000 to 5,000**; poaching, livestock grazing and habitat loss cut them to about **150 by 1970**. Project Hangul pushed numbers above 340, then they fell again to under 200 in 2004. The 2025 census counted **323**, most in **Dachigam National Park**, just above Srinagar. It is listed as Critically Endangered. Females rarely survive to breed in numbers, and leopards and stray dogs take fawns.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's last wild red deer, and its count is a health check for Kashmir's forests.
spotlights.memory_hook: 323 deer, one valley, no spare.

sections.title: Pit houses, kings and philosophers
sections.intro_md:
People have lived in the Valley for at least 5,000 years. Farmers at **Burzahom** dug houses into the karewa soil around 3000 BCE. Under the Mauryas and then the **Kushans**, Kashmir became a centre of Buddhist learning; tradition places the **Fourth Buddhist Council**, under Kanishka in the 1st or 2nd century CE, at Kundalvana near Srinagar, and stamped clay tiles from the Kushan-era site at **Harwan** survive.

Then came the great Hindu dynasties, the Karkotas, Utpalas and Loharas, between the 7th and 12th centuries. **Lalitaditya Muktapida** (8th century) raided far across north India and built Martand. Kashmir's scholars produced some of the most important Sanskrit thought in India: poetics, grammar, medicine and the philosophy now called **Kashmir Shaivism**.

We know so much because one Kashmiri, **Kalhana**, sat down in the 12th century and wrote the history of his country in verse, checking temple inscriptions and land grants as he went.

spotlights.name: Burzahom
spotlights.spot_it: A grassy terrace above Dal Lake with roped-off circular pits and a few tall standing stones.
spotlights.story_md: Neolithic farmers here lived in round **pit dwellings** dug up to several metres into the compact karewa soil, some with steps, probably to escape the winter cold. In a later phase they buried their dead under their floors, often in a crouched position, sometimes with **dogs** and antlers laid beside them. Some skulls carry **drilled holes**, a sign of trepanation, surgery on the living skull. A stone slab shows a hunting scene with two bright objects in the sky that some astronomers have read as one of the oldest records of a supernova; others are unconvinced. Archaeologists also found links to Neolithic China in its harvesting knives.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest known settlement in the Valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: Houses dug into the ground, dogs buried with masters.

spotlights.name: Rajatarangini, the river of kings
spotlights.spot_it: A Sanskrit verse chronicle, usually seen in Sharada-script manuscripts or Aurel Stein's 1900 English edition.
spotlights.story_md: **Kalhana**, son of a minister, composed about 7,800 verses in eight books, called *tarangas* or waves, tracing Kashmir's kings from legend to his own day. What makes it unusual is method: he says he consulted eleven earlier works, temple inscriptions, coins and land grants, and he judges kings harshly. The early books are legend; from the 7th century on, his account matches other evidence well. Later writers, **Jonaraja** and **Shrivara**, continued it into the sultanate. Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin had it translated into Persian, and the Hungarian-British scholar **Aurel Stein** produced the classic English translation in 1900.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is often called the first true work of history written in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: One poet, eight waves, a thousand years of kings.

spotlights.name: Martand Sun Temple
spotlights.spot_it: Massive grey limestone ruins on a plateau: a roofless central shrine with a trefoil arch, ringed by a colonnade of fluted pillars.
spotlights.story_md: **Lalitaditya Muktapida** built this temple to **Surya**, the sun god, in the 8th century. The complex is about 67 m by 43 m: a central shrine inside a courtyard lined with **84 small cells** and fluted columns that look almost Greek, a style historians trace to Gandharan, Gupta and even Syrian influences. Later Kashmiri chroniclers blamed **Sultan Sikandar** (1389 to 1413) for its destruction; modern historians warn those accounts may exaggerate, and earthquakes did their share. The ASI protects it as a monument of national importance. It appeared in the 2014 film *Haider*, which some Kashmiri Pandits objected to.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the grandest ruin of Hindu Kashmir.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sun temple with Greek-looking columns in a Himalayan valley.

spotlights.name: Abhinavagupta
spotlights.spot_it: Remembered as a seated sage teaching students, in later devotional paintings; no portrait from life exists.
spotlights.story_md: Abhinavagupta was a Kashmiri philosopher and critic whose ideas still shape Indian art theory. His **Tantraloka** is the great synthesis of **Kashmir Shaivism**, a non-dual philosophy in which the world is the free play of consciousness. His commentary on the *Natyashastra*, the **Abhinavabharati**, explained **rasa**, the aesthetic emotion an audience tastes, and argued hard for **shanta rasa**, peace, as a ninth. Every Bharatanatyam teacher who explains rasa today is using his frame. Legend says he walked into the Bhairava cave near Srinagar with his disciples and never came out.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made Kashmir the capital of Indian aesthetics for a thousand years.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Kashmiri who taught India what art feels like.

sections.title: Sultans, saints and a poet-queen
sections.intro_md:
In **1339** a courtier named **Shah Mir** took the throne and founded the Kashmir Sultanate, which lasted, under Shah Miri and then Chak rulers, until **Akbar** annexed the Valley in **1586**. Islam spread slowly, mostly through Sufi preachers rather than conquest. The Persian scholar **Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani** arrived in the 1370s and 1380s with hundreds of followers, and craftsmen in his train are credited with the shawl and other crafts.

The period produced Kashmir's two founding poets, a Shaiva woman mystic and a Muslim Sufi who admired her, and the Valley's own blend of faith, which Kashmiris later called **Kashmiriyat**: shrines visited by both communities, saints claimed by both.

It was not all gentle. **Sultan Sikandar** (1389 to 1413) is remembered for breaking temples and persecuting Brahmins. His son, **Zain-ul-Abidin**, reversed almost all of it.

spotlights.name: Lal Ded (Lalleshwari)
spotlights.spot_it: Imagined in paintings as an older woman ascetic, hair loose, often barely clothed; her short verses are called vakhs.
spotlights.story_md: Lalla, born into a Pandit family near Srinagar in the early 14th century, left an unhappy marriage in her twenties and wandered the Valley as an ascetic. About **285 vakhs**, four-line verses in early Kashmiri, are credited to her, making her one of the first poets of the language. They mock empty ritual and look for God within. Hindus call her **Lalleshwari** or Lal Yogini; Muslims call her **Lal Arifa**, the knowing one. A popular legend says she persuaded the infant Nund Rishi to take his mother's milk. Kashmiris still quote her lines in daily speech, often without knowing whose they are.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is the mother of Kashmiri poetry and a saint for both faiths.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lalla went naked into poetry and came out a saint for two faiths.

spotlights.name: Nund Rishi and Charar-e-Sharief
spotlights.spot_it: A wooden shrine with a tiered pagoda-like roof in a hill town; Nund Rishi's sayings, called shruks, quoted on walls.
spotlights.story_md: **Sheikh Nur-ud-Din Wali**, called Nund Rishi or Alamdar-e-Kashmir, the flag-bearer of Kashmir, founded the **Rishi order**, a homegrown Sufi tradition of vegetarian, tree-planting hermits. His line *ann poshi teli, yeli wan poshi*, food will last only as long as the forests, is now painted on Forest Department signboards. His shrine at **Charar-e-Sharief** is the most important in the Valley. In **May 1995**, during a standoff between militants and the Army, the 600-year-old wooden shrine and much of the town burned down; it has since been rebuilt.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave Kashmir a saint who preached ecology 600 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Food lasts as long as the forests: a saint's warning on a forest board.

spotlights.name: Khanqah-e-Moula (Shah-e-Hamadan)

where.label: Srinagar old city, on the Jhelum

spotlights.spot_it: A tiered wooden building on the Jhelum bank with a pyramidal roof topped by a spire, its walls covered in painted papier-mache panels.
spotlights.story_md: Built in memory of **Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani**, the Persian preacher Kashmiris call **Shah-e-Hamadan**, this khanqah (Sufi hospice) is one of the oldest mosques in Srinagar. Burned twice, it was rebuilt in 1732. It is the best place to see Kashmir's wooden mosque style: log-crib walls, a stacked pagoda roof that sheds snow, and no dome. Inside, every surface is carved, painted and lacquered in the papier-mache and khatamband styles Hamadani's followers are said to have brought. Non-Muslims may visit the outside; the interior is often closed to visitors.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Kashmir built Islam in wood, not stone.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mosque that looks like a pagoda and is painted like a jewel box.

spotlights.name: Jamia Masjid, Srinagar
spotlights.spot_it: A vast brick courtyard mosque with four pagoda-roofed towers and a forest of tall deodar pillars inside.
spotlights.story_md: Sultan Sikandar began it in **1394**. Fire destroyed it three times; the present building dates mainly from Aurangzeb's reign. Its roof rests on **378 deodar pillars**, each a single tree trunk, some about 15 m tall. Around **33,000** can pray inside, and on Fridays in Ramadan up to about 100,000 fill it and the lanes. It has been closed more than once: the Sikh governors banned prayers from **1819** for about 24 years, and after August 2019 restrictions lasted 136 days. Its pulpit is the seat of the **Mirwaiz**, the hereditary head preacher, now Umar Farooq.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the political and spiritual heart of downtown Srinagar.
spotlights.memory_hook: 378 tree trunks hold up the roof.

spotlights.name: Zain-ul-Abidin, the Budshah
spotlights.spot_it: A brick tomb with a domed roof in Srinagar's old city, beside the tomb of his mother, built on a temple plinth.
spotlights.story_md: Kashmiris call him **Budshah**, the Great King. Son of the temple-breaking Sikandar, he did the opposite: he abolished the **jizya** tax on non-Muslims, invited Pandits who had fled to return, let temples be rebuilt and Hindu law apply to Hindus, and patronised music his father had banned. He spent years in **Samarkand** as a youth, and craftsmen from there helped him develop **papier-mache**, paper making, carpet weaving and khatamband ceilings in Kashmir. His translation bureau put the *Mahabharata* and the *Rajatarangini* into Persian. He built **Zaina Kadal** bridge and Zainalanka island.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of the crafts Kashmir sells today trace to his court.
spotlights.memory_hook: The sultan who undid his father.

spotlights.name: Habba Khatoon
spotlights.spot_it: Her name is on a pyramid-shaped peak in Gurez and in songs still sung at weddings: lyrics of longing called lol.
spotlights.story_md: A village girl named Zoon, the moon, from near Pampore, Habba Khatoon became the wife of **Yusuf Shah Chak**, the last independent sultan. In **1586** the Mughal emperor **Akbar** lured Yusuf Shah to his court and exiled him to Bihar, where he died. Habba Khatoon is said to have wandered the Valley singing for him. Her songs, in the **lol** form of lyric longing, are among the most loved in Kashmiri. A peak in **Gurez** is named after her, and a story says she rested at its spring. Historians note that early chronicles barely mention her and much of her life comes from later tradition.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She gave Kashmiri its voice of loss at the moment Kashmir lost its independence.
spotlights.memory_hook: A queen singing for a king exiled to Bihar.

sections.title: Paradise gardens, then a kingdom for sale
sections.intro_md:
The Mughals loved Kashmir as a summer retreat. **Jahangir**, who died on his way back from it, is said to have asked for nothing but Kashmir as he lay dying. The emperors and their nobles laid out terraced gardens along Dal Lake, fed by mountain springs, with water running down a central channel through cascades and fountains.

Mughal rule faded in the 1750s. Afghan **Durrani** governors (1752 to 1819) are remembered for harsh taxes; **Ranjit Singh's** Sikh empire (1819 to 1846) was no gentler for Muslim peasants, and famine struck in the 1830s.

Then, after the first Anglo-Sikh war, the British did something unusual: in **1846** they sold the Valley. The buyer was **Gulab Singh**, a Dogra raja of Jammu who had served the Sikhs and stayed neutral in the war. His family ruled Jammu and Kashmir for the next 101 years, from palaces at Mubarak Mandi in Jammu and Sher Garhi in Srinagar.

spotlights.name: Shalimar Bagh

where.label: Northeast shore of Dal Lake, Srinagar

spotlights.spot_it: A long terraced garden with a central water channel, rows of fountains and chinars, ending in a black stone pavilion over a waterfall.
spotlights.story_md: **Jahangir** laid out Shalimar in **1619** for his wife **Nur Jahan**, on three terraces about 12 hectares in all, climbing away from the lake. The top terrace, once for the women of the court, holds a **black marble pavilion** standing in a pool, with niches called **chini khanas** behind the waterfalls where oil lamps glowed through the water at night. A Persian couplet, *if there is paradise on earth, it is here, it is here, it is here*, is linked to the garden. Shah Jahan later copied the name for his Shalimar in Lahore. The nearby **Nishat Bagh**, built by Nur Jahan's brother Asif Khan in 1633, has 12 terraces, often said to stand for the zodiac.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the template for the Mughal garden across the subcontinent.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paradise has a waterfall and a black stone room.

spotlights.name: Treaty of Amritsar, 1846
spotlights.spot_it: A short treaty in English and Persian; in portraits, Gulab Singh is a bearded Dogra raja in a jewelled turban.
spotlights.story_md: Under the treaty, the East India Company transferred "all the hilly or mountainous country" between the **Indus** and the **Ravi**, including the Kashmir Valley, to **Gulab Singh** for **75 lakh Nanakshahi rupees**. Each year, as a sign of British supremacy, he had to send **one horse, twelve shawl goats and three pairs of Kashmiri shawls**. Kashmiri nationalists later called it the *sale deed* of Kashmir and its people. Gulab Singh's dynasty went on to add Ladakh, Gilgit and Baltistan, building the largest princely state in British India by area.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created the borders that India and Pakistan still fight over.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole valley sold for 75 lakh, a horse, twelve goats and six shawls.

sections.title: 1947 to 2019: accession, conflict, and a special status undone
sections.intro_md:
In **1947** Maharaja **Hari Singh**, a Hindu ruler of a Muslim-majority state bordering both new dominions, hoped to stay independent. In October, tribal raiders from Pakistan's North-West Frontier swept toward Srinagar, looting Baramulla. Hari Singh signed the **Instrument of Accession** to India and Indian troops were flown into Srinagar on **27 October**. The war ended on **1 January 1949** with a UN ceasefire line, later the **Line of Control**, which still divides the old state: India holds Jammu, the Valley and Ladakh; Pakistan holds Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan; China holds Aksai Chin.

Inside India, the state got **Article 370**, its own constitution and flag. Wars followed in 1965 and 1971. After a disputed state election in **1987**, an armed insurgency broke out in 1989, backed from Pakistan. Tens of thousands died over the next three decades, including civilians, militants and security forces; estimates of the total range from about 40,000 to over 70,000.

On **5 August 2019** Parliament revoked the special status and split the state into two union territories.

Simla Agreement renames the ceasefire line the Line of Control

First assembly election as a UT; Omar Abdullah chief minister

spotlights.name: Hari Singh and the Instrument of Accession
spotlights.spot_it: A printed form filled in by hand, signed "Hari Singh"; in photos, the maharaja wears a turban with a plume and a military jacket.
spotlights.story_md: The document is dated **26 October 1947**, but historians argue about when Hari Singh signed it: some say 25, others 27 October, after Indian troops had already landed. The timing matters because Pakistan argued the accession was a fraud. **Lord Mountbatten** accepted it on 27 October and wrote that the question should be settled "by a reference to the people" once order returned, which became the root of the plebiscite demand. The instrument gave India only defence, foreign affairs and communications. Hari Singh left Kashmir in 1949 and died in Bombay in 1961.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the legal basis of India's claim to Jammu and Kashmir.
spotlights.memory_hook: One signature, one airlift, seventy-eight years of argument.

spotlights.name: Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah
spotlights.spot_it: A very tall man in a karakuli cap and a long coat; his mausoleum stands at Hazratbal.
spotlights.story_md: A schoolteacher from Soura who led protests against the maharaja from 1931, Abdullah founded the party that became the **National Conference** and was called **Sher-e-Kashmir**, the lion of Kashmir. As prime minister of the state from 1948, he carried out one of Asia's most radical land reforms: in 1950 the **Big Landed Estates Abolition Act** took land above about 22.75 acres from landlords without compensation and gave it to tillers. In **1953** Nehru's government had him arrested; he spent most of the next 11 years in prison. He returned as chief minister in 1975. His son Farooq and grandson **Omar** have both been chief ministers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He shaped modern Kashmir's politics and its land.
spotlights.memory_hook: The lion of Kashmir who gave land to the tiller and went to jail.

spotlights.name: Article 370
spotlights.spot_it: A short article of the Constitution titled "Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir".
spotlights.story_md: Article 370 let the state keep its own constitution and limited Parliament's powers there to what the state accepted. A 1954 order added **Article 35A**, letting the state define permanent residents, who alone could buy land and hold state jobs. On **5 August 2019** a presidential order and a parliamentary resolution made almost all of it inoperative; a Reorganisation Act created the two union territories. A long security lockdown followed, and mobile internet stayed cut for months, one of the longest shutdowns in any democracy. On **11 December 2023** a five-judge Supreme Court bench upheld the move, told the government to restore statehood "as soon as possible", and ordered elections by September 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its removal ended seven decades of special status.
spotlights.memory_hook: Temporary provision, lasting seventy years.

spotlights.name: Exodus of Kashmiri Pandits

where.label: Kashmir Valley to Jammu and Delhi

spotlights.spot_it: Rows of one-room tenements at Jagti and Muthi camps near Jammu, built for families who left the Valley.
spotlights.story_md: As the insurgency grew in 1989 and 1990, militants killed Pandit officials, judges and activists, and threatening posters and slogans spread fear. Between January and March **1990**, most of the Valley's Kashmiri Hindu population left, mainly for Jammu and Delhi. Scholars estimate that **90,000 to 100,000** left in the first months, out of 120,000 to 140,000, and over 150,000 over the decade; some community figures are higher. Estimates of Pandits killed range from **about 220** (government, 1989 to 2004) to several hundred (community groups). Kashmiri Hindus mark **19 January** as Exodus Day. Few have returned, though thousands of young Pandits have taken government jobs in the Valley under a 2008 package.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It emptied the Valley of a community that had lived there for millennia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three months in 1990 that a community still counts its life from.

sections.title: Kashmiri, Dogri and a script that nearly died
sections.intro_md:
Under the **Jammu and Kashmir Official Languages Act, 2020**, the territory has five official languages: **Kashmiri, Dogri, Hindi, Urdu and English**. Before 2020, Urdu and English alone did the government's work, and Kashmiri, spoken by half the population, was barely taught.

**Kashmiri** (Koshur) belongs to the Dardic group of Indo-Aryan languages, with sounds no other Indian language has. It was written in **Sharada** for centuries, then in a Perso-Arabic script that is official today. **Dogri**, the language of the Jammu hills, was once written in **Takri**, a cousin of Sharada; now it uses Devanagari. It entered the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution in **2003**. In the hills, **Gojri** and **Pahari** are spoken by herding and mountain communities.

The 2011 census found Kashmiri the mother tongue of **52.9%**, Dogri **20.5%**, Gojri **9.5%** and Pahari **8%**.

spotlights.name: Sharada script
spotlights.spot_it: Angular letters with a flat top line, often on brown birch-bark leaves, as in the Bakhshali manuscript.
spotlights.story_md: Sharada, named after the goddess of learning, was Kashmir's script for Sanskrit and early Kashmiri for about a thousand years. Kashmiri scholars wrote on **birch bark** (*bhojpatra*), which survives surprisingly well; many of the oldest Sanskrit manuscripts in European libraries are Kashmiri birch-bark texts in Sharada. The **Bakhshali manuscript**, with one of the earliest uses of a dot for zero, is written in a form of Sharada. Today only some Kashmiri Pandit priests still read it for horoscopes and rituals. It was encoded in Unicode in 2012, and enthusiasts run online classes to keep it alive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It held Kashmir's written memory for a millennium.
spotlights.memory_hook: Birch bark, a flat top line, and the earliest zero.

spotlights.name: Dogri and the Dogras
spotlights.spot_it: A soft hill language heard in Jammu's bazaars; Dogra men in old photos wear tight churidar and long angarkhas with turbans.
spotlights.story_md: The **Dogras**, Hindu and Sikh Rajputs, Brahmins and others of the Jammu hills, take their name, tradition says, from the land of two lakes, **Mansar and Surinsar**. The Dogra regiment of the Indian Army draws on them. Dogri literature includes the modern poet **Padma Sachdev**, who wrote lyrics for Lata Mangeshkar, and the language now has a Sahitya Akademi award. Its old script, **Takri**, was used by Dogra kings for land records and coins. Dogri was added to the Constitution's Eighth Schedule in **2003** and made an official language of the territory only in **2020**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the second language of the territory and the core of Jammu's identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two lakes, one people, one language.

spotlights.name: Agha Shahid Ali
spotlights.spot_it: A Kashmiri-American poet in photos, smiling, scarf around the neck; known for ghazals in English.
spotlights.story_md: Born in New Delhi and raised in Srinagar, Agha Shahid Ali taught in the United States and became the poet who carried Kashmir into English. **The Country Without a Post Office** (1997) is about Kashmir in the early 1990s, when mail and news stopped. He championed the **ghazal** in English, with its fixed rhyme and repeated refrain, and edited the anthology *Ravishing DisUnities*. His collection *Rooms Are Never Finished* was a finalist for the US National Book Award in 2001, the year he died of brain cancer. His poem lines appear on walls and banners in Srinagar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave the Kashmir of the 1990s its most quoted voice in English.
spotlights.memory_hook: A country without a post office, written down in ghazals.

sections.title: Shrines on mountains, springs and lake shores
sections.intro_md:
Faith in Jammu and Kashmir climbs. Hindus walk 12 km uphill to **Vaishno Devi** and up to 43 km over high passes to the ice cave of **Amarnath**. Muslims gather at **Hazratbal** on Dal Lake to see a relic of the Prophet. In between lie hundreds of Sufi shrines, called **ziarats** or **astans**, where Kashmiris of every background tie threads and light candles.

The Valley's Islam was shaped by Sufis and its Hinduism by Shaiva philosophy and the cult of the goddess. For centuries the two shared saints and festivals: Muslim families kept the Amarnath route and the Kheer Bhawani spring, Hindu families visited the Rishi shrines. That shared culture is what people mean by **Kashmiriyat**. The conflict since 1989 strained it badly, but it shows up every year at Kheer Bhawani, where Muslim neighbours still sell milk and flowers to returning Pandit pilgrims.

Jammu, by contrast, is a temple city, and its shrine economy is one of the biggest in India.

spotlights.name: Vaishno Devi

where.label: Trikuta hills, above Katra, Reasi district

spotlights.when: Cave shrine of great age; Shrine Board since 1986
spotlights.spot_it: A lit-up shrine complex hugging a mountainside above Katra, with a 12 km paved path full of pilgrims chanting 'Jai Mata Di'.
spotlights.story_md: The goddess is worshipped as three natural rock forms, the **pindis** of Maha Kali, Maha Lakshmi and Maha Saraswati, inside a cave at about **1,585 m**. In 1986 the state took control from hereditary priests and set up the **Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board**, which built the path, shelters and helipad. Pilgrim numbers rose from about 14 lakh that year to a peak of over **1 crore in 2011**; about 95 lakh came in 2023, making it one of the most visited shrines in India. On **26 August 2025** a landslide at **Adhkuwari**, halfway up, killed about 35 pilgrims after days of record rain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the economic engine of Katra and much of Jammu.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three stones, twelve kilometres, a crore of pilgrims.

spotlights.name: Amarnath cave
spotlights.spot_it: A gaping cave mouth in a bare mountain at 3,888 m, lines of pilgrims and ponies below, and inside a pillar of ice.
spotlights.story_md: Inside the cave, dripping water freezes into a tall **ice stalagmite** that pilgrims worship as a **Shiva lingam**; it grows through spring and shrinks by late summer. Popular tradition says a Muslim shepherd, **Buta Malik**, found the cave in the 19th century, and his family long shared in the offerings. Pilgrims walk either about 43 km from **Pahalgam** via Sheshnag lake, or about 14 km from **Baltal**, steeper and shorter. Several lakh people make the yatra each summer under heavy security, carried by local pony-wallahs, porters and tent-keepers who earn much of their year's income in six weeks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Valley's largest pilgrimage, and a large seasonal economy for Muslim villagers.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lingam of ice that grows and melts each year.

spotlights.name: Hazratbal Shrine

where.label: North shore of Dal Lake, Srinagar

spotlights.when: Relic arrived about 1700; present building 1968 to 1979
spotlights.spot_it: A gleaming white marble mosque with a single dome and minaret on the Dal Lake shore, unlike the pagoda-roofed wooden mosques around it.
spotlights.story_md: The shrine keeps the **Moi-e-Muqaddas**, a hair believed to be from the Prophet Muhammad's beard. Tradition says a merchant, **Khwaja Nur-ud-Din Eshai**, acquired it and that it reached Kashmir around 1700. It is shown to the public on special days, when tens of thousands gather. On **27 December 1963** the relic disappeared, Srinagar erupted in protest, and it was recovered on 4 January 1964. The present white marble building, finished in **1979**, has the only big dome among the Valley's major shrines. In September 2025, a plaque with India's national emblem inside was smashed, setting off a political row.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Kashmir's holiest Muslim shrine.
spotlights.memory_hook: One hair, one white dome, one week the Valley held its breath.

spotlights.name: Kheer Bhawani (Tulmul)
spotlights.when: Mela on Jyeshtha Ashtami, May or June
spotlights.spot_it: A small white marble temple standing in a spring-fed pool, the water tinted, pilgrims pouring milk and rice pudding into it.
spotlights.story_md: The goddess **Ragnya Devi** is worshipped at a spring in the village of **Tulmul**. Devotees offer **kheer**, rice pudding, which gives the shrine its name. Kashmiri Pandits believe the spring changes colour to foretell the future: milky white or rose for good times, dark or black for disaster; many say it turned dark before 1990. The big **mela** falls on Jyeshtha Ashtami. Even after the exodus, thousands of Pandits return each year, and their Muslim neighbours set up stalls selling milk, flowers and candles, and put up water points for pilgrims.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most important annual meeting of displaced Pandits with their old home.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spring that changes colour to warn.

sections.title: Santoor, satire and a women's dance in rows
sections.intro_md:
Kashmir's classical music is **Sufiana Kalam**, Sufi poetry sung to a set of modes called **maqams**, which came with Persian and Central Asian musicians from the 15th century. Its instruments are the **santoor**, a hammered dulcimer, the long-necked **saz-e-Kashmir** and **setar**, and the **wasool** drum. Folk music runs on the **rabab**, the **tumbaknari**, a tall clay drum played at weddings, and on the songs women sing in turns called **wanwun**.

The Valley also has a 500-year-old tradition of travelling satirists, the **Bhand Pather** players, and a gentle women's dance, **Rouf**.

Jammu has its own forms: **Kud**, a night-long dance of thanks to local deities in the hills, and the **Dogri** folk songs of the Shivaliks. The best-known musician from the territory, though, made his name in Mumbai, by taking a Kashmiri folk instrument and making it classical.

spotlights.name: Rouf
spotlights.when: Spring, Ramadan nights, Eid and weddings
spotlights.spot_it: Two rows of women facing each other, arms linked around shoulders, swaying forward and back with small steps as they sing in turn.
spotlights.story_md: Rouf is danced by women, in two lines facing each other. Each line links arms and moves with a slow, rocking step, a small kick of the foot, while singing a verse that the other line answers. There are no instruments: the voices and the footwork are the music. It is danced in spring, at weddings, and above all on the nights of **Ramadan** and at **Eid**, when girls gather in courtyards. The songs are often by Habba Khatoon or other Kashmiri poets. Schoolgirls perform staged versions at state functions, but it lives mostly in homes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Valley's most widely danced folk form, kept alive by women.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two rows of linked arms, rocking like a boat.

spotlights.name: Santoor and Shivkumar Sharma
spotlights.spot_it: A trapezoid wooden box strung with about 100 strings, played by tapping with two light walnut-wood hammers; it sounds like rain on water.
spotlights.story_md: The santoor came to Kashmir from Persia and was used to accompany Sufiana singing. **Shivkumar Sharma**, born in **Jammu** in 1938, was set on it by his father, a singer, and spent decades changing the instrument, its tuning and its playing technique so it could hold a full Hindustani raga. His 1967 album **Call of the Valley**, with flautist **Hariprasad Chaurasia** and guitarist Brij Bhushan Kabra, sold worldwide. As the duo **Shiv-Hari**, he and Chaurasia scored Hindi films including *Silsila* (1981) and *Chandni* (1989). He received the Padma Vibhushan in 2001 and died in 2022.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned a Kashmiri folk instrument into a concert instrument heard worldwide.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hundred strings, two walnut hammers, rain on a lake.

spotlights.name: Bhand Pather
spotlights.when: Old folk theatre, at least several centuries
spotlights.spot_it: Actors in loud costumes and masks performing in an open courtyard, led by a piercing surnai oboe and a dhol, mocking a landlord or a foreign officer.
spotlights.story_md: **Bhands**, hereditary performers from villages such as **Akingam** and **Wathora**, perform **pathers**, short plays of satire. Each pather has a stock theme: *Raja Pather* mocks the king, *Angrez Pather* the British officer who cannot speak Kashmiri, *Darza Pather* the tax man, *Shikargah Pather* the hunt, with actors in animal masks. The music comes from the **surnai**, a shrill oboe. The bhands often play as Muslim performers at a Shiva shrine in Akingam, an old link between the two faiths. Their audience shrank sharply during the conflict, and revival groups now stage it at festivals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how Kashmiri villagers mocked their rulers for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Laugh at the king, then pass the hat.

sections.title: Shawls, papier-mache and a painted Krishna with beetle wings
sections.intro_md:
Kashmir's crafts were built for export long before the word existed. The Kashmir shawl was one of the luxury goods of the Mughal and Persian world; in the late 18th century it reached Europe, where Napoleon's wife **Josephine** owned hundreds of them, weavers in **Paisley** in Scotland copied the curled **boteh** motif, and the copy gave the pattern its English name.

Most crafts are said to have come with Persian Sufis or with **Zain-ul-Abidin's** Samarkand craftsmen: shawls, papier-mache, carpets, khatamband ceilings and walnut carving. Several now carry **Geographical Indication** tags: Kashmir Pashmina, Kani shawl and Sozani embroidery among the first in 2008, followed by papier-mache, walnut wood carving and khatamband, and hand-knotted carpets.

Jammu's hills produced something else: **Pahari miniature painting**, which began in tiny courts such as **Basohli** on the Ravi and spread to Kangra and Guler.

visual.title: Some J&K crafts and foods with GI tags

spotlights.name: Basohli painting
spotlights.spot_it: Hot red borders, flat saffron-yellow or green backgrounds, large almond-shaped eyes, and tiny glittering green dots that are pieces of beetle wing.
spotlights.story_md: In the late 17th century, painters at the small hill court of **Basohli** produced one of the boldest styles in Indian art. The famous **Rasamanjari** series, one set dated 1694 to 1695 and signed by the painter **Devidasa**, illustrates a Sanskrit poem on lovers with Krishna as the hero. To mimic emeralds in jewellery, painters glued on tiny cut pieces of **iridescent beetle wing**. Basohli was the first school of **Pahari** painting; within a century its fierce colours had softened into the lyrical Kangra style. Basohli painting received a GI tag in 2023, and the Met in New York and other museums hold pages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the opening chapter of Pahari painting, one of India's great miniature traditions.
spotlights.memory_hook: Krishna in a red frame, jewels made of beetles.

spotlights.name: Pashmina

where.label: Srinagar workshops; goats in Changthang, Ladakh

spotlights.when: Shawl trade from at least the 16th century; GI 2008
spotlights.spot_it: A soft, light, matte shawl that warms instantly; hand-spun yarn is slightly uneven, and real pashmina has a faint musty smell when it burns.
spotlights.story_md: Pashmina comes from the fine winter underfleece of the **Changthangi goat**, raised by nomads at 4,000 m and above on the Changthang plateau of Ladakh and Tibet. The fibre is about **12 to 16 microns**, finer than a human hair, which is about 70. In Kashmir women spin it by hand on a wheel called a **yinder**, and men weave it on hand looms. A finer cousin, **shahtoosh**, came from the endangered Tibetan antelope, killed for its wool; its trade has been banned internationally since 1975 and in J&K since the early 2000s. The famous **ring test**, pulling a shawl through a finger ring, was for shahtoosh and proves little about pashmina.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Valley's signature luxury, and a living for tens of thousands of spinners and weavers.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goat at 4,000 metres, a woman at a wheel, a shawl through a ring.

spotlights.name: Kani shawl
spotlights.spot_it: A shawl covered edge to edge in woven, not embroidered, paisley and floral patterns, slightly ribbed on the back where coloured threads switch.
spotlights.story_md: Kani weavers do not use a shuttle. They use dozens to hundreds of small wooden bobbins called **kanis** or tujis, each wound with a coloured yarn, and interlock them by hand across each row, following a coded pattern called the **talim**, written in a shorthand that a reader calls out like music. A complex shawl may take one or two weavers a year or more, at a few centimetres a day. The village of **Kanihama** is the centre. This was the shawl that crossed to Europe in the 18th century; when Jacquard looms in Paisley and Lyon copied it cheaply, Kashmir's shawl economy collapsed in the 1870s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the technical summit of Kashmiri weaving.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hundreds of bobbins, a coded song, a year per shawl.

spotlights.name: Kashmiri papier-mache
spotlights.spot_it: Lacquered boxes, vases and Christmas baubles painted with dense chinar leaves, birds and flowers in bright colours and gold.
spotlights.story_md: The craft has two stages. **Sakhtsazi**: waste paper is soaked, pounded with rice glue and moulded over a form, then dried and smoothed. **Naqashi**: master painters add base colour, gold or silver leaf and fine designs with brushes made from cat or kid-goat hair, then varnish. The motifs, *hazara* (a thousand flowers), *gul-andar-gul*, and the chinar leaf, come from shawl designs. Much of the work is now Christmas ornaments sold to Europe and the United States. The same painters decorated the ceilings of Shah-e-Hamadan and old Srinagar homes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns wastepaper into one of Kashmir's best-known exports.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paper pulp in, a thousand flowers out.

spotlights.name: Walnut wood carving
spotlights.spot_it: Dark, polished furniture and screens carved deep with chinar leaves, lotus, grapes and dragons, sometimes cut right through as lattice.
spotlights.story_md: Kashmiri walnut (*Juglans regia*) is dense, close-grained and takes deep undercut carving. Carvers in Srinagar work in four styles: **undercut** (deep, layered relief), **open or jaali** (pierced lattice), **semi-carving**, and **shallow** carving. The best pieces use wood from the root and lower trunk, which has the darkest colour. Because walnut trees are protected for their nuts, felling needs a permit, and good timber has become scarce. A trunk is seasoned for years before carving. Pieces made for 19th-century British buyers, carved tables and screens, now sell at antique auctions.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most skilled of Kashmir's wood crafts.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tree too valuable to cut, carved too deep to copy.

spotlights.name: Kashmir willow cricket bats
spotlights.spot_it: Stacks of pale bat blanks, called clefts, drying in the sun in pyramids by the Srinagar to Jammu highway in Anantnag.
spotlights.story_md: Along the highway near **Sangam** and **Bijbehara**, hundreds of small units cut willow trunks into clefts, season them and shape them into bats. Kashmir willow is the same species as English willow, *Salix alba*, but grows in a different climate; it is generally harder and heavier, and far cheaper. Most cricket bats used in Indian gullies and school grounds come from here. Makers say the trade was hurt by a shortage of willow, as orchards replaced trees, and by the 2019 lockdown; some have since moved upmarket, selling to international players.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of India's cricket starts with a bat from one district of Kashmir.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's gully cricket is made in Anantnag.

sections.title: Thirty-six courses, pink tea and the red gold of Pampore
sections.intro_md:
Kashmiri cooking has two great traditions. **Muslim** cooking, crowned by the wedding feast called **wazwan**, uses onions, shallots, dried **Kashmiri chilli** for colour, and a lot of mutton. **Kashmiri Pandit** cooking, equally meat-loving, avoids onion and garlic and leans on **asafoetida**, dried ginger powder (*sonth*) and fennel; its rogan josh tastes quite different. Both love **haak**, collard greens, and **nadru**, lotus stem.

The day starts with the **kandur**, the neighbourhood baker, and salty pink tea. Rice, not wheat, is the staple. Winter food is dried: vegetables, fish and even tomatoes are sun-dried in autumn to eat in Chillai Kalan.

Jammu eats differently: **rajma chawal**, especially with the small red kidney beans of **Bhaderwah**, which got a GI tag in 2023; **kalari**, a fried mountain cheese; **kaladi kulcha**; and Dogra feasts called **dham**. The territory also grows almost all of India's saffron.

spotlights.name: Wazwan
spotlights.when: Wedding feast; tradition of Central Asian origin
spotlights.spot_it: Four guests sharing one big copper plate, the trami, heaped with rice and topped with kebabs and ribs, with bowls of red and white meatball curries arriving in turn.
spotlights.story_md: A full wazwan can run to **36 courses**, nearly all of them meat, cooked overnight in big copper pots over wood fires by hereditary cooks called **wazas**, under a master, the **vasta waza**. Guests sit in fours around a **trami**. An attendant brings the **tash-t-nari**, a jug and basin, to wash hands. Seven dishes are considered essential, among them **tabak maaz** (fried ribs), **rista** (meatballs in red gravy), **rogan josh** and **gushtaba**, soft meatballs in yoghurt gravy that close the meal. The meat for rista and gushtaba is pounded by hand with wooden mallets on stone until it is almost a paste.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the centre of every Kashmiri Muslim wedding and the region's most famous food.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four people, one plate, thirty-six courses, gushtaba last.

spotlights.name: Noon chai, kahwa and the samovar
spotlights.spot_it: A pink, salty, milky tea poured from a brass or copper samovar, and a clear golden green tea with saffron strands and almond slivers.
spotlights.story_md: **Noon chai** (*noon* means salt in Kashmiri) is made by boiling green tea leaves with a pinch of **baking soda** for a long time, then adding cold water, milk and salt. The soda and the long boil turn it a striking **pink**. Kashmiris drink it two or three times a day with bread from the kandur. **Kahwa**, for guests and for cold days, is green tea brewed with **saffron**, cardamom, cinnamon and almonds, usually sweetened. Both are served from the **samovar**, a metal urn with a central tube holding live coals, a Central Asian tool that came over the trade routes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the drink of Kashmiri daily life and hospitality.
spotlights.memory_hook: Green leaves, a pinch of soda, and the tea turns pink.

spotlights.name: Pampore saffron
spotlights.when: Harvest late October to early November; GI 2020
spotlights.spot_it: Fields on flat karewa terraces turned violet for two weeks in autumn, families bent picking crocus flowers into wicker baskets.
spotlights.story_md: The saffron crocus flowers for only a couple of weeks a year. Each flower has three red stigmas, picked by hand and dried; it takes roughly **150,000 flowers** to make one kilogram. Kashmir's crop grows on the **karewa** of Pampore and nearby villages, which supply over 90% of India's saffron. Kashmiri saffron got a **GI tag in 2020**. But the area under it has shrunk from about **5,700 hectares** in the late 1990s to around 3,700, and output has fallen hard, from about 15 tonnes to a few tonnes in bad years, because of erratic rain, irrigation problems and land sold for housing. Iran grows most of the world's saffron.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most valuable crop per gram in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: 150,000 flowers for one kilo of red gold.

spotlights.name: The kandur, Kashmir's neighbourhood baker
spotlights.spot_it: A small shop with a clay tandoor sunk in the floor, a baker slapping dough onto its walls, men in pherans waiting with cloth bags.
spotlights.story_md: Every Kashmiri neighbourhood has a **kandur**, and most families buy bread twice a day: **tsot** or **girda**, a round bread with finger marks pressed in, for morning tea; **lavasa**, a thin flatbread; **kulcha**, crumbly and sesame-topped; and the flaky **bakarkhani** for special days. The baker is usually up by 4 am. The queue at the kandur is where neighbourhood news travels, and in times of curfew people judged how bad things were by whether the kandur had opened. In winter, some families still bring their own dough or pots of meat to slow-cook in the cooling oven.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first social stop of every Kashmiri day.
spotlights.memory_hook: No breakfast in Kashmir without the kandur's girda.

sections.title: How people live: fire pots, houseboats and herders on the move
sections.intro_md:
Life in the Valley is organised around winter. Before Chillai Kalan, families stock dried vegetables, firewood and charcoal; houses have a sitting room with thick carpets where everyone gathers around the warmth. The real heater, though, is personal: a clay **kangri** under a woollen **pheran**.

Family ties are tight and joint households common. Weddings run several days, with women singing **wanwun** in call-and-response and a henna night called **maenzraat**. Fertility has fallen fast: the National Family Health Survey 2019 to 2021 found about **1.4 children per woman**, well below replacement and among the lowest in India. Schooling for girls has risen sharply in a generation.

On the move each spring and autumn are more than a million **Gujjars** and **Bakarwals**, Scheduled Tribes who herd buffalo, goats and sheep between Jammu's plains and the high meadows. And on the water, Srinagar keeps a way of living that began as a legal trick.

spotlights.name: Pheran and kangri
spotlights.spot_it: A long, loose, wide-sleeved woollen gown down to the shins; under it, a bulge where a wicker-wrapped clay pot of embers is held against the body.
spotlights.story_md: The **pheran** is a loose woollen robe worn by men and women, wide enough to hold a **kangri** inside: a small clay pot filled with glowing charcoal, wrapped in woven willow wicker with a handle. People carry it to work, to the mosque and into bed. A Kashmiri saying holds that what Laila was to Majnun, the kangri is to a Kashmiri. Doctors in the 19th century described **kangri cancer**, a skin cancer on the belly and thighs caused by years of heat. Electric heaters are common now, but power cuts keep the kangri in use; **Charar-e-Sharief** makes the most prized ones.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most Kashmiri object there is: a portable fire.
spotlights.memory_hook: A gown with a fire inside.

spotlights.name: Houseboats of Dal and Nigeen
spotlights.spot_it: Long wooden boats with carved cedar verandas, names like 'New Buckingham Palace' painted on the side, moored in rows.
spotlights.story_md: Under the Dogra maharajas, outsiders, including the British, could not buy land in Kashmir. So British visitors and officers in the late 19th century had houses built on the water. The result is the Srinagar **houseboat**: a cedar hull with carved walnut and khatamband interiors, chandeliers, a sitting room and bedrooms, served by a family living on a smaller boat behind. At their peak there were well over a thousand; now there are under 1,000, many in poor repair, because building new boats has long been banned to protect the lakes. Guests reach them by **shikara**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is how a land law created Kashmir's most famous hotel.
spotlights.memory_hook: Can't own the land? Live on the lake.

spotlights.name: Bakarwal migration
spotlights.when: April to May up, September to October down
spotlights.spot_it: Families on foot with goats and sheep, horses carrying tents and children, crossing high passes under snow peaks.
spotlights.story_md: **Bakarwals** (from *bakri*, goat) are Gojri-speaking nomadic herders, mostly Muslim, recognised as a **Scheduled Tribe** in 1991. Each spring families leave the warm plains of Jammu, Kathua and Rajouri and walk their flocks for weeks over the **Pir Panjal**, to summer pastures in Kashmir and beyond, then return in autumn. The routes cross passes above 4,000 m. Changing land use, new roads and forest rules have narrowed their paths, and the government now runs trucks to move some families and flocks. Their sheepdogs, the **Bakarwal mastiff**, are a rare breed guarding flocks against bears and leopards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are one of South Asia's last great walking migrations.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twice a year, a whole community walks over the mountains.

sections.title: People to know: from the slopes to the stadium
sections.intro_md:
Many of the territory's best-known people appear elsewhere today: Lal Ded, Habba Khatoon, Agha Shahid Ali, Kalhana, Abhinavagupta, Sheikh Abdullah and Shivkumar Sharma. Others worth knowing: **Karan Singh**, Hari Singh's son, regent at 18 and later a Union minister; **Mehbooba Mufti**, the first woman chief minister (2016 to 2018); the poet **Mahjoor** (1887 to 1952), who turned Kashmiri verse from mystic to political; and Dogri poet **Padma Sachdev**.

Sport has two firsts. **Arif Khan**, a skier from Tangmarg below Gulmarg, was India's only athlete at the **2022 Beijing Winter Olympics**, entering the slalom and giant slalom. And a cricketer from Bijbehara, near the willow bat factories, became the first from J&K to play for India.

spotlights.name: Parvez Rasool
spotlights.spot_it: A right-handed batsman and off-spinner in J&K colours, from the same district as Kashmir's bat makers.
spotlights.story_md: Parvez Rasool was the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to play in the **IPL** (2013, Pune Warriors) and to play for **India**, making his ODI debut against Bangladesh in 2014 and later playing a T20 international against England in 2017. He captained J&K in the Ranji Trophy and won the Lala Amarnath award for best all-rounder in domestic cricket. He grew up in Bijbehara, near the willow bat factories, practising on rough local grounds.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He opened the door for J&K cricketers such as Umran Malik and Abdul Samad.
spotlights.memory_hook: From the bat-making district to an India cap.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Most visitors see the **Srinagar, Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg** circuit, and the pilgrims' Jammu and Katra. That leaves much of the territory unseen. Worth the effort: **Doodhpathri** and **Yusmarg**, meadows south-west of Srinagar; **Aharbal** waterfall on the Vishav river; the springs and Mughal gardens of **Verinag** and **Achabal**; **Bhaderwah**, called mini Kashmir, in the Jammu hills; **Patnitop** and the lakes of **Mansar** and **Surinsar**; and the old Dogra town of **Ramnagar** with its painted palace.

New tunnels have changed access. The **Chenani to Nashri** tunnel (9.2 km, 2017) bypasses Patnitop on the Jammu highway, and the **Z-Morh** tunnel (2025) keeps Sonamarg open in winter. Some sites near Pahalgam closed after the April 2025 attack; the government reopened many in 2026.

Best seasons: April for tulips and almond blossom, June to August for meadows and treks, late October for chinars and saffron, January to March for snow.

spotlights.name: Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden
spotlights.when: Opened 2007; blooms late March to April
spotlights.spot_it: Long terraced bands of red, yellow, pink and purple tulips under the Zabarwan hills, Dal Lake in the distance.
spotlights.story_md: Opened in **2007** to stretch the tourist season into spring, the garden covers about **30 hectares** on the slopes of the Zabarwan range and is called the **largest tulip garden in Asia**. It plants around **1.7 million bulbs** of more than 70 varieties, plus hyacinths, daffodils and ranunculus, and opens for about a month. It drew about **4.3 lakh visitors** in 2024. Because tulip bulbs need cold, the garden's display depends on a proper winter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made April a tourist season in Kashmir.
spotlights.memory_hook: 1.7 million bulbs for one month of colour.

spotlights.name: Sonamarg and the Z-Morh tunnel
spotlights.spot_it: A long green valley floor along the Sindh river with glaciers at its head, and the road climbing on toward the Zojila pass.
spotlights.story_md: Sonamarg, the meadow of gold, at about 2,800 m, is the last stop before the **Zojila** pass to Ladakh and a base for treks to the Thajiwas glacier and the great lakes of Gangabal. For generations it was cut off by snow all winter. The 6.5 km **Z-Morh tunnel**, named for the zigzag road it replaces, opened on **13 January 2025** and keeps Sonamarg reachable year-round. In October 2024, during its construction, militants attacked the workers' camp at Gagangir and killed seven people. The longer **Zojila tunnel**, about 14 km, is being built beyond it to give Ladakh an all-weather road.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the gateway to Ladakh and to the Valley's best treks.
spotlights.memory_hook: A zigzag road replaced by a straight tunnel.

spotlights.name: Gurez
spotlights.when: Opened more widely to visitors since 2021
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow valley of log houses beside a turquoise river, with a sharp pyramid-shaped mountain, Habba Khatoon peak, above it.
spotlights.story_md: Gurez lies on the **Kishanganga** river, known as the Neelum on the Pakistani side, right on the Line of Control, reached over the 3,300 m Razdan pass, which is shut by snow for months. Its people are **Dards** who speak **Shina**, not Kashmiri, and build houses of stacked logs. The valley was on the old Silk Route branch from Kashmir to Gilgit. Shelling made it a no-go area for years; after the India-Pakistan ceasefire of February 2021 tourism grew. The 330 MW **Kishanganga** hydro project diverts the river's water through a tunnel into the Jhelum basin, which Pakistan contested at the Court of Arbitration.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a different culture tucked inside Kashmir, on the frontier.
spotlights.memory_hook: Log houses, Shina speech, a peak named for a poet-queen.

sections.title: How it earns: apples, tourists and rivers
sections.intro_md:
Jammu and Kashmir's economy is small: its gross product was estimated at over **₹2.3 lakh crore** in 2023 to 2024, and the 2026 to 2027 budget projection was about ₹3.15 lakh crore. Government is the biggest employer, and the territory depends heavily on central grants.

The three private engines are **horticulture**, **tourism** and **handicrafts**. Apples alone are said to support about 3.5 million people and contribute around 10% of the territory's output. Tourism hit a record in 2024, with about **35 lakh** visitors to the Valley alone, before the April 2025 attack.

The rivers are the other asset. The Chenab, Jhelum and their tributaries could generate around 20,000 MW of hydropower; only a fraction is built. And in **February 2023** the Geological Survey of India reported an inferred **5.9 million tonnes** of lithium ore resources at **Salal-Haimana** in Reasi district, the first such find in India, though auctions in 2023 and 2024 drew no successful bidder.

data.label: Apples
data.note: Around 2 million tonnes in good years

spotlights.name: Kashmir's apple orchards
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of trees heavy with red Delicious apples, wooden crates stacked by the roadside, trucks queued for the highway.
spotlights.story_md: J&K grows about **three-quarters of India's apples**, around 2 million tonnes in good years, mostly in **Shopian, Sopore, Baramulla and Kulgam**. The **Sopore fruit mandi** is one of the biggest in Asia. Old orchards grow tall varieties such as Red Delicious and the local **Ambri**; growers are now switching to **high-density** dwarf trees from Italy and the Netherlands that fruit in two or three years. The weak link is the road: when the Srinagar to Jammu highway closes, trucks get stuck for days and fruit spoils. Since the railway reached the Valley in 2025, growers have started sending some apples by **rail** as well.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the biggest private livelihood in the Valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three of every four Indian apples come from here.

spotlights.name: Baglihar Dam and the Indus Waters Treaty
spotlights.spot_it: A concrete gravity dam across the steep Chenab gorge, its spillway gates open in a white curtain of water.
spotlights.story_md: Baglihar is a **900 MW** run-of-the-river project on the Chenab. Under the 1960 **Indus Waters Treaty**, the western rivers, Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, were allotted mostly to Pakistan, with India allowed run-of-river hydropower. Pakistan objected to Baglihar's design; in 2007 a World Bank neutral expert largely sided with India. After the Pahalgam attack in **April 2025**, India declared the treaty **in abeyance**, and in May flushed silt from Baglihar and Salal reservoirs without notice to Pakistan. New projects on the Chenab, such as Pakal Dul and Ratle, are being pushed faster.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It sits at the centre of India and Pakistan's water dispute.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dam that turned a treaty into a weapon.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The past two years have been among the most turbulent in the territory's recent history.

**Politics.** The October 2024 election returned an elected government for the first time since 2018, but a union territory government has limited powers; police and public order sit with the Lieutenant Governor. Restoring **statehood** is the defining demand. On **28 September 2026** the assembly passed a resolution asking Delhi for immediate statehood; BJP members walked out. The government restored the **Darbar Move** in autumn 2025.

**Security.** On **22 April 2025** gunmen killed 26 people, mostly tourists, at Baisaran meadow near Pahalgam. India struck targets in Pakistan in **Operation Sindoor** on 7 May; four days of fighting ended in a ceasefire on 10 May, after Pakistani shelling killed civilians in Poonch and other border towns.

**Weather.** In August 2025 a cloudburst at Chositi in Kishtwar killed about 68 people, and a landslide on the Vaishno Devi route killed about 35.

**Tourism.** Early 2026 brought crowds back to Gulmarg and reopened sites; by May, the trade said recovery was still uneven.

spotlights.name: The Pahalgam attack
spotlights.spot_it: A wide meadow ringed by pine forest above Pahalgam, reachable only on foot or by pony, now closely guarded.
spotlights.story_md: Baisaran, called mini Switzerland by guides, is a meadow about 5 km above Pahalgam. On the afternoon of **22 April 2025**, gunmen came out of the forest and shot tourists, singling out men; **26 people** died, 25 tourists and a local pony operator, **Syed Adil Hussain Shah**, who was killed trying to grab a gun from an attacker. The Resistance Front, linked to Lashkar-e-Taiba, first claimed and then disowned it. Kashmiris held candlelight marches and shut shops in protest, an unusually united response. India suspended the Indus Waters Treaty and, on 7 May, launched Operation Sindoor.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reshaped India-Pakistan relations and emptied Kashmir's tourist season.
spotlights.memory_hook: A meadow, a pony man who fought back, and a war four days long.

spotlights.name: The statehood demand

where.label: Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly, Srinagar

spotlights.spot_it: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah speaking in the assembly; banners reading 'Statehood is our right' at National Conference rallies.
spotlights.story_md: When the Supreme Court upheld the 2019 changes it took the government's word that statehood would return, but set no date. The National Conference won the 2024 election promising it. **Omar Abdullah**, grandson of Sheikh Abdullah, leads that push. His cabinet passed a statehood resolution in October 2024; in **July 2026** his party protested in Delhi; and on **25 September 2026** he moved a resolution in the assembly, passed on **28 September** with about 60 of 90 members in support. It is not binding. Delhi has repeatedly said statehood will come at an appropriate time.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the political question that will define the territory's next few years.
spotlights.memory_hook: A state demoted to a territory, asking to be promoted back.

sections.title: Myths, facts and a recap
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: Kashmir is all snow.** The Jammu plains reach about 45 °C in June.

**Myth: Article 370 stopped Indians from visiting Kashmir.** Anyone could visit and rent. It, with Article 35A, reserved land purchase and state jobs for permanent residents, much as Himachal Pradesh and the northeast still protect land.

**Myth: Kashmiri Hindus and Muslims were always enemies.** They shared saints, shrines and a language for centuries; the bitter split dates mainly from 1989 to 1990.

**Myth: rogan josh is red from tomatoes.** The colour comes from mild Kashmiri chillies and **mawal**, cockscomb flower.

**Recap.** A drained lake; a Dogra hill country; a thousand years of Sanskrit learning; Sufi saints and a poet-queen; a kingdom sold for 75 lakh; seven decades of special status and conflict; and now a territory joined by rail, asking to be a state again.

quiz_bank.prompt: What are kanis, in a Kani shawl?
quiz_bank.explanation: Small wooden bobbins, each with one colour of yarn.

quiz_bank.prompt: What did Basohli painters glue on to look like emeralds?
quiz_bank.explanation: Pieces of iridescent beetle wing.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which dish traditionally ends a wazwan?
quiz_bank.explanation: Gushtaba, meatballs in yoghurt gravy.

quiz_bank.prompt: What turns noon chai pink?
quiz_bank.explanation: Baking soda and a long boil, then milk.
options: Baking soda and a long boil

quiz_bank.prompt: Where does a Kashmiri carry a kangri?
quiz_bank.explanation: Under the pheran, against the body.

quiz_bank.prompt: Why did the British build houseboats in Srinagar?
quiz_bank.explanation: The Dogra maharajas did not let outsiders buy land.

quiz_bank.prompt: Arif Khan was India's only athlete at the 2022 Winter Olympics.
quiz_bank.explanation: He competed in slalom and giant slalom.

quiz_bank.prompt: Parvez Rasool was the first J&K cricketer to:
quiz_bank.explanation: Play for India (and in the IPL).

quiz_bank.prompt: Srinagar's tulip garden plants roughly how many bulbs?
quiz_bank.explanation: About 1.7 million.

quiz_bank.prompt: What does the Z-Morh tunnel do?
quiz_bank.explanation: Keeps Sonamarg open in winter.

quiz_bank.prompt: Which town has one of Asia's biggest fruit markets?
quiz_bank.explanation: Sopore.

quiz_bank.prompt: After the Pahalgam attack, India put which treaty in abeyance?
quiz_bank.explanation: The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty.

quiz_bank.prompt: Who was the local man killed at Baisaran trying to stop an attacker?
quiz_bank.explanation: Syed Adil Hussain Shah, a pony operator.

quiz_bank.prompt: The J&K assembly's statehood resolution of September 2026 is legally binding on Delhi.
quiz_bank.explanation: It is a demand, not binding; Parliament must legislate.

quiz_bank.prompt: Article 370 made it illegal for other Indians to visit Kashmir.
quiz_bank.explanation: It restricted land purchase and state jobs, not visits.
