best_facts.fact: The Chenab Rail Bridge deck stands 359 m above the river, higher than the top of the Eiffel Tower, and was designed with the DRDO to survive a blast of about 40 tonnes of TNT.
best_facts.why_surprising: A bridge designed against bombs as well as wind.

best_facts.fact: In 1846 the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh for 75 lakh rupees plus an annual tribute of one horse, twelve shawl goats and three pairs of shawls.
best_facts.why_surprising: A valley and its people sold like an estate.

best_facts.fact: Noon chai turns pink because green tea leaves are boiled with a pinch of baking soda; Kashmiris drink it with salt, not sugar.
best_facts.why_surprising: Green leaves make a pink, salty tea.

best_facts.fact: The British built Srinagar's houseboats because the Dogra maharajas would not let outsiders buy land, so they lived on the lake instead.
best_facts.why_surprising: A land law created Kashmir's most famous hotels.

best_facts.fact: For nearly 150 years the government of J&K physically moved, files and all, between Srinagar and Jammu twice a year; it was ended in 2021 and restored in 2025.
best_facts.why_surprising: A capital that packs its bags.

best_facts.fact: Kalhana's Rajatarangini, finished in 1149, is often called the first true history written in India because he checked inscriptions and land grants.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 12th-century poet who did archival research.

best_facts.fact: Basohli painters glued tiny pieces of iridescent beetle wing onto their pages to look like emeralds.
best_facts.why_surprising: Insects as jewellery on a painting.

best_facts.fact: Doctors in the 19th century documented kangri cancer, a skin cancer caused by Kashmiris carrying fire pots against their bodies all winter.
best_facts.why_surprising: A heater so personal it left a medical trace.

best_facts.fact: Nund Rishi said food would last only as long as the forests in the 15th century, and the line is now on Forest Department signboards.
best_facts.why_surprising: Ecology preached by a Sufi 600 years ago.

best_facts.fact: Kani shawl weavers follow a coded pattern called the talim, read aloud like a song, interlocking hundreds of tiny wooden bobbins by hand.
best_facts.why_surprising: Weaving by reading a musical code.

best_facts.fact: Burzahom's Neolithic people lived in pits dug into the ground, sometimes buried dogs with their dead, and drilled holes in some skulls.
best_facts.why_surprising: Stone Age surgery and pet burials above Dal Lake.

best_facts.fact: It takes about 150,000 crocus flowers to make one kilogram of saffron, and Pampore supplies over 90% of India's crop.
best_facts.why_surprising: Red gold, picked one flower at a time.

best_facts.fact: Srinagar's Jamia Masjid was closed to prayers for about 24 years under Sikh rule and for 136 days after August 2019.
best_facts.why_surprising: A mosque whose closures map Kashmir's politics.

best_facts.fact: The hangul fell from perhaps 5,000 to about 150 by 1970; the 2025 count found 323.
best_facts.why_surprising: A deer saved from the edge, but only just.

best_facts.fact: Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin, son of a temple-breaking father, abolished jizya, invited Pandits back and had the Mahabharata translated into Persian.
best_facts.why_surprising: The son who reversed his father.

best_facts.fact: Kashmir willow is the same species as English willow; the difference in bats comes from climate and seasoning, and most of India's gully cricket bats come from Anantnag.

side_dish.title: How to build an arch from both sides of a gorge
side_dish.body_md:
An arch carries load by pushing outward and downward into its supports, so every piece is squeezed rather than bent. That is why stone and steel arches can span so far. The problem is building one where there is nothing underneath.

Over a river you can sometimes put up temporary scaffolding, called **falsework**, and build the arch on top. Over a 359 m deep gorge with a fast river, you cannot. The Chenab bridge builders used **cantilever construction**: each half of the steel arch was built out from its own bank, piece by piece, held up by steel cables running back over tall temporary towers to anchors in the rock. Each new segment was lifted into place by a cable crane strung across the gorge.

For years the two halves hung in the air, getting closer, each supported only by its cables. The hardest moment is **closure**: the two tips must meet within millimetres, even though steel grows and shrinks with temperature through the day. Engineers often close an arch at a set time, usually early morning, when the temperature matches their calculations. The Chenab arch closed in April 2021. Once joined, the arch carries itself, and the cables come off.

The same idea, cantilevers meeting in the middle, built the Sydney Harbour Bridge in 1930.

offline_task.title: Make Kashmiri kahwa
offline_task.body_md:
Kahwa is the Kashmiri tea for guests. You need green tea, whole spices and, ideally, a few strands of saffron.

**For 2 cups:** bring 2 cups of water to a boil with a 3 cm piece of cinnamon, 2 lightly crushed green cardamom pods and 2 cloves. Simmer for 5 minutes. Add a pinch of saffron (4 to 6 strands). Turn off the heat, add 1 teaspoon of loose green tea, cover and steep for 2 minutes only, or it turns bitter. Strain into cups with a teaspoon of honey or sugar each, and float a few slivers of almond on top.

Notice the colour: the saffron turns it gold. In Kashmir it comes from a samovar with coals inside, and it is drunk after a heavy meal or on a cold afternoon.

If you want to try noon chai instead, you will need gunpowder green tea and baking soda, and about 30 minutes of boiling; the pink colour only comes after the long boil and the cold-water shock.
